title: While I Was
overview: Tell a longer story about the past. Say what you were doing when something cut across it: I was cooking when the power went off. Learn the past of eight verbs you cannot work out, and name the exact place and day inside the sentence. Then read an incident record, write your own account of what happened, and say it out loud.
learningPath: The lesson: listen once with the page open, then again.
Words: listen, look and say. 30 words in 4 groups.
Patterns: 4 cards. Read the worked example before the practice.
Reading: read texts 1 and 2. Keep the record in text 3 for the questions.
Speaking: 6 tasks. Tap the mic, say it, listen back, check.
Writing: 4 tasks. Plan, write, then check your own lines.
Practice: 1 to 6, each with a key and a score line.
Quiz: 12 questions. Last, the assignment card.
lectureScript:
Hello. This is Unit 12.
This unit is about telling a longer story about the past.
Not one sentence. A whole account, with the detail that makes it clear.
First, eight past forms you cannot work out.
You already know worked, played and stopped. Those add -ed.
These eight do not.
teach becomes taught. throw becomes threw. spend becomes spent.
build becomes built. hide becomes hid.
shake becomes shook. wear becomes wore. lead becomes led.
There is no rule under them. You learn them one by one.
Say each pair out loud, twice: teach, taught. Throw, threw.
And watch one thing. After did, the verb goes back to its plain form.
She taught me. But: Did she teach you?
Second, one action cutting across another.
You can already say what you were doing: I was cooking.
Now something cuts across it.
I was cooking when the power went off.
The long action takes was or were and -ing.
The short action that cuts in takes the past form.
So: was cooking, and went.
Two small words hold this together.
Use when in front of the short action: when the power went off.
Use while in front of the long one: while I was cooking.
Both sentences say the same thing.
I was cooking when the power went off.
While I was cooking, the power went off.
When the while part comes first, put a comma after it.
Ask yourself one question. Which one was already running?
That one takes was or were and -ing.
Third, naming the exact place and the exact time.
Somebody asks you: which shop? which day?
You can answer inside the same sentence.
Use where for a place: the shop where I bought it.
Use when for a time: the day when it happened.
The shop where I bought it was near the station.
I still remember the morning when the lift stopped.
No commas go inside these parts.
They tell the reader which one you mean, so nothing can be taken out.
Fourth, the small words.
One account needs four kinds of them at once.
When? At six. On Monday. In the morning. During the shift.
Where? In the yard. At the entrance. On the roof.
Exactly where? Under the stairs. Behind the fence. At the top of the steps.
Which way? Into the building. Out of the basement. Up the stairs. Towards the exit.
Ask the four questions in that order, and the sentence builds itself.
Now the words.
Thirty of them, in four groups.
The eight verbs: teach, throw, spend, build, hide, shake, wear, lead.
What happened: scene, event, incident, trouble, situation, solution, detail, consequence.
Where it happened: doorway, entrance, exit, stairs, roof, yard, basement, fence.
And the words that put it in order: previously, shortly, briefly, meanwhile, beforehand, initially.
In this unit you read an account of one wet Monday morning.
You read an incident record that somebody filled in at a desk.
You write your own account in four parts.
Then you check it, one line at a time, four times over.
Then you tell it out loud in two minutes and listen back.
Take one card at a time. Say every line.
Let us start.

outcomes.outcome: Name exactly which place and which time you mean inside the sentence: the shop where I bought it, the day when it happened.
outcomes.evidence: Pattern 3 practice, six of eight; Practice 3 self-checked; Writing 2 against its five points; Quiz items 3 and 10.

outcomes.outcome: Choose the right small word for time, place, position and direction inside one account.

outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can say when and where it happened: at six, in the yard, up the stairs.

words.meaning: To show somebody how to do something, so that they can do it too.
words.example: She teaches the new staff every Monday.
practice: She taught me the job in two days.
Who taught you to drive?
I did not teach him that.
He teaches at a school near the market.
words.tutor: Tell the tutor one thing somebody taught you at work, or where you study. Use taught, and listen for it in the answer you get back.

words.meaning: To send something through the air with your hand.
words.example: Throw the empty bottle in the bin.
practice: I threw the broken glass away.
She threw the box out into the yard.
Do not throw anything from the roof.
Who threw this paper on the floor?
words.tutor: Ask the tutor for three sentences with threw. Say each one back and listen to the start of the word.

words.meaning: To use time or money on something.
words.example: I spend an hour on the bus every day.
practice: We spent an hour at the entrance, waiting.
She spent all morning on one form.
How much did you spend?
Do not spend long on this part.
words.tutor: Say two sentences with spent: one about time and one about money. Ask the tutor which one is which.

words.meaning: To make something by putting parts together.
words.example: They build houses on this street.
practice: They built the fence last summer.
Who built this shelf?
I did not build it, and I cannot fix it.
They built the basement before the rest of the building.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor for the past form of build, then for five more verbs whose past form ends in t.

words.meaning: To put something where nobody can see it.
words.example: Hide the key somewhere safe.
practice: He hid the key under the step.
Where did you hide the tools?
I hid the money in a book and then I forgot it.
Do not hide the trouble: tell the desk.
words.tutor: Say one sentence with hid and a place word in it: under, behind or inside. Ask the tutor to repeat the place word back.

words.meaning: To move quickly from side to side.
words.example: The wind shakes that door every night.
practice: The whole door shook in the wind.
My hands shook after the incident.
Shake the bottle before you open it.
The bus shook as it went over the bridge.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor for three things that shake. Say what makes each one shake.

words.meaning: To have clothes, or something like a helmet, on your body.
words.example: You wear a helmet on this floor.
practice: I wore a helmet all morning.
What did she wear?
He wore the same uniform for ten years.
Everybody in the basement wears a helmet.
words.tutor: Say what you wore yesterday and what you are wearing now. Ask the tutor whether wore and wearing were in the right places.

words.meaning: To go in front and show other people the way.
words.example: The manager leads the group to the exit.
practice: She led us out of the basement.
Who led the shift that day?
This door leads to the stairs.
He did not lead them the right way.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor for the past form of lead, and for one sentence where lead means a door going somewhere.

words.meaning: Everything you could see at the place where something happened.
words.example: The manager arrived at the scene in two minutes.
practice: Start with the scene: where you were, and when.
Nobody moved anything at the scene.
The scene was wet and dark.
Describe the scene in one sentence.
words.tutor: Describe the scene where you are sitting now in two sentences: where, and when.

words.meaning: Something that happens, especially something important.
words.example: One small event changed the whole morning.
practice: Put the events in order, first to last.
The event lasted two minutes.
Two events happened at the same time.
Which event do you remember best?
words.tutor: Tell the tutor about one event from last week in three sentences. Ask it whether your order was clear.

words.meaning: Something bad or unusual that happens, often quickly.
words.example: The incident was over by half past eight.
practice: Report the incident at the desk on the same day.
There was an incident in the yard this morning.
Nobody was hurt in the incident.
Write the time of the incident on the form.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor for the difference between an event and an incident, with one example of each.

words.meaning: A problem, or a difficult time.
words.example: We had trouble with the lift all week.
practice: The trouble started at the entrance.
I had trouble finding the exit.
Tell the desk if there is any trouble.
What kind of trouble was it?
words.tutor: Say one sentence with trouble and one with problem. Ask the tutor whether both sound natural to it.

words.meaning: How things are at one moment, especially when there is a problem.
words.example: The situation was simple: the doors could not close.
practice: Explain the situation in two sentences.
The situation got worse after the rain.
In this situation, press the button and wait.
What was the situation when you arrived?
words.tutor: Describe one difficult situation, real or made up, in three sentences. Ask the tutor to ask you one question about it.

words.meaning: The thing that ends a problem.
words.example: The solution took her one minute.
practice: There is a simple solution: take the box out.
Nobody had a solution that morning.
Write the trouble on the left and the solution on the right.
What was your solution?
words.tutor: Tell the tutor a problem, real or made up. Ask it for two possible solutions, then say which one you would choose and why.

words.meaning: One small piece of information about something.
words.example: One detail makes the whole account clear.
practice: The detail I remember is the open box.
Write every detail on the form.
Do not give ten details: give one.
Which detail tells you it was raining?
words.tutor: Ask the tutor to tell you a short story, then to ask you three questions about small details in it.

words.meaning: Something that happens later because of something else.
words.example: The incident had one consequence: everybody used the stairs.
practice: Every action has a consequence.
The consequence of the rain was a wet floor.
What was the consequence for the staff?
That was the only consequence.
words.tutor: Say one thing that happened and one consequence of it. Ask the tutor to join them into one sentence.

words.meaning: The open space where a door is.
words.example: I was standing in the doorway with a wet bag.
practice: Never leave a box in a doorway.
She waited in the doorway of the office.
The doorway was too narrow for the desk.
Who is standing in the doorway?
words.tutor: Ask the tutor for the difference between a door and a doorway, with one example of each.

words.meaning: The way into a building or a place.
words.example: We waited at the entrance for ten minutes.
practice: The entrance is at the front of the building.
Meet me at the entrance at six.
There is a notice by the entrance.
Which entrance did you use?
words.tutor: Describe the entrance to a building you know: where it is, and what you see there.

words.meaning: The way out of a building or a place.
words.example: I carried the bag towards the exit.
practice: The exit is at the back, past the stairs.
Keep the exit clear at all times.
She led us to the nearest exit.
Where is the exit on this floor?
words.tutor: Ask the tutor to describe a room and say where the exit is. Then say the same thing back in your own words.

words.meaning: The steps that take you from one floor of a building to another.
words.example: The stairs were wet all morning.
practice: I walked up the stairs to the fourth floor.
She was walking down the stairs when the lift stopped.
Do not run on the stairs.
The tools are at the top of the stairs.
words.tutor: Say three sentences about stairs: one with up, one with down, and one with at the top of.

words.meaning: The top of a building, on the outside.
words.example: There is water on the roof after every storm.
practice: Never throw anything from the roof.
The rain came through the roof.
Two people were working on the roof.
How do you get to the roof?
words.tutor: Ask the tutor for three things you might find on the roof of a building.

words.meaning: An open space with a wall or a fence round it, beside a building.
words.example: She threw the box out into the yard.
practice: We leave the car in the yard behind the building.
The yard was empty at six in the morning.
I carried the bag across the yard.
Is there a way out of the yard?
words.tutor: Describe a yard you know. Say what is in it and what goes round it.

words.meaning: The floor of a building that is below the ground.
words.example: The tools are in the basement.
practice: She led us out of the basement.
It is cold and dark in the basement.
I went into the basement to find a box.
There was water in the basement after the storm.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor what people usually keep in a basement, then say whether that is true in a building you know.

words.meaning: A wall of wood or metal that goes round a yard or a garden.
words.example: They built the fence last summer.
practice: He hid the box behind the fence.
The fence is too high to climb.
The fence goes all the way round the yard.
Who paid for the fence?
words.tutor: Ask the tutor for three things a fence is for. Then say which one matters most, and why.

words.meaning: Before the time you are talking about.
words.example: Previously, nobody noticed how wet that floor was.
practice: She previously worked in the same building.
Previously, the exit was on the other side.
I did not know that previously.
What did you do previously?
words.tutor: Say one sentence about now and one about previously. Ask the tutor to check that the second verb is in the past.

words.meaning: Soon, a short time after or before something.
words.example: Shortly after that, the doors opened.
practice: The manager arrived shortly afterwards.
Shortly before six, it started to rain.
The bus leaves shortly.
Shortly after the incident, they put a notice up.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor for two sentences with shortly after and two with shortly before. Say which ones come earlier.

words.meaning: For a short time, or in few words.
words.example: Explain briefly what happened.
practice: The lights went out briefly and came back on.
She spoke briefly to the desk.
Briefly, the box stopped the doors closing.
Tell me briefly, in two sentences.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor to tell you a long story. Then tell it back briefly, in three sentences, and ask what you left out.

words.meaning: At the same time as something else.
words.example: Meanwhile, everybody else was using the stairs.
practice: I waited in the lift. Meanwhile, the cleaner found the box.
She was washing the floor. Meanwhile, it started to rain.
Meanwhile, nothing happened at the entrance.
What was happening meanwhile?
words.tutor: Say two things that were happening at the same time. Join the second one with meanwhile.

words.meaning: Before something happens, and ready for it.
words.example: Check the stairs beforehand, not afterwards.
practice: Nobody looked at the doorway beforehand.
Fill the form in beforehand and bring it with you.
Beforehand, I did not know the exit was locked.
Did you read it beforehand?
words.tutor: Ask the tutor for the difference between beforehand and previously, with one example of each.

words.meaning: At the start, before things changed.
words.example: Initially, nobody knew why the lift stopped.
practice: Initially, the doors did not open at all.
I initially thought it was the rain.
The plan initially had five steps.
Initially, this feels slow.
words.tutor: Say what you initially thought about something and what you think now. Ask the tutor to check both verbs.

grammar.title: Taught, threw, spent, hid: eight to remember
grammar.explanation:
You already make the past with -ed: worked, played, stopped.
Eight verbs in this unit do not do that.
They change shape, and there is no rule under the change.
teach becomes taught. hide becomes hid.
You learn these one by one, out loud, in pairs.
grammar.rule:
The verb now, then the verb in the past:
teach, taught: She taught me the job in two days.
throw, threw: I threw the empty box in the bin.
spend, spent: We spent an hour at the entrance.
build, built: They built the fence last summer.
hide, hid: He hid the key under the step.
shake, shook: The whole door shook in the wind.
wear, wore: I wore a helmet all morning.
lead, led: She led us out of the basement.

For not, use did not and the plain verb:
I did not spend long there.
She did not wear a helmet.

For a question, use did and the plain verb:
Did she teach you the job?
Where did you hide the key?

The past form appears only where there is no did.
grammar.workedExample:
You want to say that this person showed you the job last week.
1. Which verb do you need? teach.
2. Is it finished? Yes, last week. So it is the past.
3. teach does not take -ed. Its past form is taught.
4. She taught me the job last week.
5. Now say it did not happen. After did not the verb is plain again: She did not teach me the job.
6. Now ask it: Did she teach you the job?
7. taught appears in line 4 only, because line 4 is the one with no did in it.
grammar.mistake:
It is easy to add -ed to these: teached, throwed, hided.
English does not: taught, threw, hid.
The other slip is keeping the past form after did.
No: Did she taught you?
Yes: Did she teach you?
did already carries the past, so the verb beside it stays plain.
grammar.tip: Say the pair, never the single word: teach, taught. Throw, threw. Hide, hid. Eight pairs said out loud beat any rule.
grammar.practice:
Write the past form of the verb in brackets.
1. She ______ (teach) me the job in two days.
2. I ______ (throw) the broken glass away.
3. We ______ (spend) an hour at the entrance.
4. They ______ (build) the fence last summer.
5. He ______ (hide) the key under the step.
6. The whole door ______ (shake) in the wind.
7. I ______ (wear) a helmet all morning.
8. Fix this line: Did she taught you the job?
grammar.answers:
1. taught
2. threw
3. spent
4. built
5. hid
6. shook
7. wore
8. Did she teach you the job?
The likeliest wrong answer is 8 left as it is. did already carries the past, so the verb beside it goes back to its plain form.
Watch 5 as well: hid has one d, not two.
6 or more right: go on. 5 or fewer: say the eight pairs out loud twice, then do 1 to 7 again.

grammar.title: The power went off while I was cooking
grammar.explanation:
One thing was already running. Another thing cut across it.
I was cooking when the power went off.
The long one takes was or were and -ing.
The short one that cuts in takes the past form.
grammar.rule:
The long one, already running:
I was cooking.
She was walking down the stairs.
They were washing the floor.

The short one, cutting across it:
the power went off
the lift stopped
somebody shouted

Put them together with when:
I was cooking when the power went off.
She was walking down the stairs when the lift stopped.

Or put while in front of the long one:
While I was cooking, the power went off.
While they were washing the floor, it started to rain.

when goes in front of the short one.
while goes in front of the long one.

The comma goes in only when the while part comes first.
grammar.workedExample:
Two things happened. You were walking down the stairs. The lights went off.
1. Which one took time? Walking down the stairs. That is the long one.
2. The long one takes was or were and -ing: I was walking down the stairs.
3. Which one was quick? The lights went off. That is the short one.
4. The short one takes the past form: went.
5. Put when in front of the short one: I was walking down the stairs when the lights went off.
6. Now turn it round with while: While I was walking down the stairs, the lights went off.
7. The while part came first here, so it takes a comma.
grammar.mistake:
It is easy to put both parts in the past form: I cooked when the power went off.
That says the cooking started because the power went off, which is not what happened.
Yes: I was cooking when the power went off.
The other slip is the comma. It goes in only when the while part comes first.
grammar.tip: Ask which one was already running. That one takes was or were and -ing.
grammar.practice:
Write the missing form.
1. I ______ (wait) at the entrance when the taxi arrived.
2. While she ______ (carry) the box, she dropped it.
3. They were washing the floor when the manager ______ (come) in.
4. We were standing in the doorway when it ______ (start) to rain.
5. Join these with when: I was cooking. The power went off.
6. Join these with while, and put the while part first: They were building the fence. It started to rain.
7. Fix this line: I cooked when the power went off.
8. Fix this line: While I was cooking the power went off.
grammar.answers:
1. was waiting
2. was carrying
3. came
4. started
5. I was cooking when the power went off.
6. While they were building the fence, it started to rain.
7. I was cooking when the power went off. The long one needs was and -ing.
8. While I was cooking, the power went off. The comma was missing.
The likeliest wrong answer is 3 written as was coming. The manager came in once, quickly, so that is the short one.
6 or more right: go on. 5 or fewer: read the worked example line by line, then do 1 to 4 again.

grammar.title: The doorway where I stood, the day when it happened
grammar.explanation:
Somebody asks you which shop, or which day.
You can answer inside the same sentence.
where names the place. when names the time.
The shop where I bought it was near the station.
grammar.rule:
A place, with where:
the shop where I bought it
the yard where the taxi waits
the building where I work
The shop where I bought it closed last month.

A time, with when:
the day when it happened
the morning when the lift stopped
the year when they built the fence
I still remember the day when it happened.

A person or a thing takes who or that:
the woman who led us out
the box that I dropped

No commas go inside these parts.
They tell the reader which one you mean, so nothing can be taken out.

The order is always the same:
the noun, then where or when, then the rest.
grammar.workedExample:
Two short lines: I bought it in a shop. The shop was near the station.
1. Which word is in both lines? shop.
2. Say it once, at the front: The shop
3. Is a shop a place or a time? A place. So use where.
4. The shop where
5. Add the rest of the first line, with no second shop: The shop where I bought it
6. Add the rest of the second line: The shop where I bought it was near the station.
7. No commas. Take the where part out and nobody knows which shop you mean.
grammar.mistake:
It is easy to say the shop where I bought it there, keeping the old place word as well.
where already means in that place, so there has to go.
No: the day when it happened then.
Yes: the day when it happened.
And keep the commas out. These parts say which one you mean, so they stay in the sentence.
grammar.tip: A place takes where. A time takes when. Say the noun, then the word, then the rest.
grammar.practice:
Write where or when, or join the two lines into one.
1. That is the building ______ I work.
2. I remember the morning ______ the lift stopped.
3. This is the yard ______ we leave the tools.
4. Nobody forgets the day ______ it happened.
5. Join these: I left my bag in a café. The café closed at six.
6. Join these: We met on a Monday. I still remember that Monday.
7. Fix this line: The shop where I bought it there was near the station.
8. Fix this line: The doorway, where I stood, was wet.
grammar.answers:
1. where
2. when
3. where
4. when
5. The café where I left my bag closed at six.
6. I still remember the Monday when we met.
7. The shop where I bought it was near the station. where already means in that place, so there goes.
8. The doorway where I stood was wet. This part says which doorway, so the commas go.
The likeliest wrong answer is 8 left with its commas. Ask yourself: can I take the part out and still know which doorway? No. So it stays, and the commas do not.
6 or more right: go on. 5 or fewer: do the worked example again, then items 5 and 6.

grammar.title: At six, in the yard, up the stairs, towards the exit
grammar.explanation:
One account needs four kinds of small word at once.
When? Where? Exactly where? Which way?
Ask the four questions in that order, and the sentence builds itself.
grammar.rule:
When? at, on, in, during
at six, at night, on Monday, in the morning, in May, during the shift

Where? at, in, on, near, outside
at the entrance, in the basement, on the roof, near the doorway, outside the building

Exactly where? under, behind, between, above, below, at the top of
under the stairs, behind the fence, between the two doors, at the top of the steps

Which way? into, out of, up, down, along, across, through, past, towards
into the yard, out of the basement, up the stairs, across the yard, towards the exit

One account, all four:
At six, in the yard, I was standing behind the fence.
Then I walked across the yard and out through the doorway.
grammar.workedExample:
You want to say this. It was six o'clock. You were in the yard. You were behind the fence. Then you walked to the exit.
1. When? Six o'clock. A clock time takes at: at six.
2. Where? The yard. A space you are inside takes in: in the yard.
3. Exactly where? Behind the fence. That is a position: behind the fence.
4. Which way? To the exit. Movement to a place takes towards: towards the exit.
5. Put the first three in that order: At six, in the yard, I was standing behind the fence.
6. Then add the movement: Then I walked towards the exit.
7. Four questions, four small words, one clear picture.
grammar.mistake:
It is easy to use in for a clock time: in six o'clock.
A clock time takes at: at six o'clock.
The other slip is using in for movement: I went in the basement.
Movement takes into: I went into the basement.
in tells the reader where you already were. into tells them where you went.
grammar.tip: Four questions, always in this order: When? Where? Exactly where? Which way?
grammar.practice:
Write the missing small word.
1. The shift started ______ six ______ the morning.
2. We waited ______ the entrance ______ Monday.
3. He put the box ______ the stairs, where nobody could see it.
4. She led us ______ of the basement and ______ the stairs.
5. I carried the bag ______ the yard and ______ the exit.
6. The tools are ______ the top ______ the stairs.
7. Fix this line: I went in the basement to find the tools.
8. Fix this line: We met in six o'clock on Monday.
grammar.answers:
1. at, in
2. at, on
3. under
4. out, up
5. across, towards
6. at, of
7. I went into the basement to find the tools. Movement takes into.
8. We met at six o'clock on Monday. A clock time takes at.
The likeliest wrong answer is 1 written as at six at the morning. Parts of the day take in: in the morning, in the afternoon, in the evening. Only at night is different.
6 or more right: go on. 5 or fewer: ask the four questions again on every line, in order.

readings.title: The Morning the Lift Stopped
readings.genre: A short account of one morning
readings.setting: A building with six floors, early on a wet Monday.
readings.passage:
It was ten past eight on Monday, and it was raining hard.
I was standing in the doorway with a wet bag, waiting for the lift.
The doors opened and I stepped in.
The lift shook once and stopped between two floors.
There was no signal on my phone.
I pressed the button beside the door, and a voice answered.
While I was waiting, I counted the minutes. There were eleven of them.
Then the doors opened, and a woman in a blue uniform led me out.
She taught me something in those two minutes on the stairs.
A lift stops for a reason, she said, and the reason is usually small.
Somebody left a box in the doorway on the fourth floor.
The doors could not close, so the lift stopped where it was.
The solution took her one minute. She threw the box out into the yard.
The incident was over by half past eight.
But it had one consequence.
Everybody in the building used the stairs that morning, and the stairs were wet.
So the manager put a notice on the wall by the entrance.
Previously, nobody noticed how wet that floor was.
That is the detail I remember now, and not the eleven minutes in the dark.
A small box in a doorway on the fourth floor changed the way the whole building walks to work.

readings.title: How to Tell Somebody What Happened
readings.setting: Anywhere you have to explain something: a desk, a phone call, a form.
readings.passage:
Somebody asks you what happened. You have one minute, and they need four things.
First, the scene. Where were you, and when? At six, in the yard, at the top of the stairs. Start there, and the person listening can see it.
Second, what was already happening. Use was or were with -ing. I was carrying a box. She was washing the floor. This is the background, and it takes four words to say.
Third, the event itself. One short sentence, in the past form. The lift stopped. The door shook. Somebody shouted.
Fourth, one detail that makes it clear. Not every detail: one. The box was open. The floor was still wet. The exit was locked.
Then say what you did about it, and what happened afterwards.
Two words help you here. Meanwhile tells the listener that something else was happening at the same time. Shortly after tells them what came next.
A good account carries no opinion in it. Say what you saw, not what you think about the person who did it.
And keep the situation and the solution apart. The situation is the trouble you were in. The solution is the thing that ended it. Put them in one sentence and the listener loses both.
Initially, this feels slow. After three or four times it is quicker than any other way, because nobody has to stop you and ask.

readings.title: Incident Record: Building 2
readings.setting: The desk inside the entrance of a building with six floors.
readings.passage:
INCIDENT RECORD
Building 2, entrance desk
Record number: 41

DATE: Monday 6 May
TIME: 08.13
PLACE: Lift 1, between floor 3 and floor 4
WRITTEN BY: the manager on the morning shift

WHAT HAPPENED
Somebody left a box in the lift doorway on floor 4. The doors could not close. Lift 1 stopped between floor 3 and floor 4, with one person inside. That person pressed the button beside the door and spoke to this desk at 08.14.

WHAT WE DID
A cleaner took the box out of the doorway at 08.22. The doors closed. Lift 1 went up to floor 4 and opened. The person walked out at 08.24.

CONSEQUENCE
The stairs were wet all morning, because of the rain. A notice now stands on the wall by the entrance.

WHAT TO DO NEXT TIME
1. Never leave anything in a lift doorway, on any floor.
2. If a lift stops, press the button beside the door and wait. Do not open the doors yourself.
3. Report the incident at the entrance desk on the same day. Do not wait for the next shift.
4. If the stairs are wet, put the notice out before you go back to work.

Records are kept for one year. Ask at the entrance desk to read this one again.

comprehension.a: Somebody left a box in the doorway on the fourth floor, so the doors could not close.
comprehension.why: The text says it twice: Somebody left a box in the doorway on the fourth floor. The doors could not close, so the lift stopped where it was.

comprehension.q: The text says the incident had one consequence. What does consequence mean here?
comprehension.a: Something that happened later because of the incident.
comprehension.why: The lines after it say what that something was: everybody used the stairs, the stairs were wet, and the manager put a notice up. All of it came after, and all of it came from the incident.

comprehension.q: The text says The solution took her one minute. What was the solution?
comprehension.a: She threw the box out into the yard.
comprehension.why: The next sentence gives it: She threw the box out into the yard. That is the thing that ended the problem, and it is what solution means here.

comprehension.q: Why were the stairs wet that morning?
comprehension.a: It was raining hard, and everybody in the building used the stairs instead of the lift.
comprehension.why: The first line says it was raining hard. The line after the consequence says everybody used the stairs. Wet people on the stairs make the stairs wet.

comprehension.q: What are the four things a listener needs, in order?
comprehension.a: The scene, what was already happening, the event itself, and one detail that makes it clear.
comprehension.why: The text numbers them First, Second, Third and Fourth, and each one gets its own short paragraph.

comprehension.q: The text says keep the situation and the solution apart. What is the difference between them?
comprehension.a: The situation is the trouble you were in. The solution is the thing that ended it.
comprehension.why: The text gives one short sentence to each, one after the other, so the two words cannot be mixed up.

comprehension.type: What a person would do next
comprehension.q: You want to say that two things were happening at the same time. Which word does the text give you?
comprehension.why: The text says Meanwhile tells the listener that something else was happening at the same time. Shortly after is the other one, and that is about what came next.

comprehension.q: The record says the lift stopped at 08.13 and the person walked out at 08.24. How long were they inside?
comprehension.why: From 08.13 to 08.24 is eleven minutes. The account in Reading 1 counts the same eleven.

comprehension.type: What a person would do next
comprehension.q: A lift stops with you inside. What does this record tell you to do?
comprehension.a: Press the button beside the door and wait, and do not open the doors yourself.
comprehension.why: Point 2 under WHAT TO DO NEXT TIME says exactly that, in two short instructions.

comprehension.q: You find a bag standing in a lift doorway on floor 2. What does this record tell you about it?
comprehension.a: Take it out of the doorway. Point 1 says never to leave anything in a lift doorway, on any floor.
comprehension.why: The record is about floor 4, but point 1 says on any floor, and WHAT HAPPENED explains why: anything in the doorway stops the doors closing.

speaking.title: Speaking 1 — Eight pairs, out loud
speaking.instructions:
Listen. Then say each pair out loud, twice.
teach, taught
throw, threw
spend, spent
build, built
hide, hid
shake, shook
wear, wore
lead, led
Now say each one inside a sentence.
She taught me the job. I threw the box away. We spent an hour there.
They built the fence. He hid the key. The door shook. I wore a helmet. She led us out.
Tap the mic. Say all eight pairs and then all eight sentences.
Tap the mic again and listen back.
Check: did you say taught and not teached?
Check: did you say hid and not hided?
Count the eight past forms you hear. Eight is the number.
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor to say the eight verbs one at a time. Say the past form back before it gives you the next one.

speaking.title: Speaking 2 — I was … when …
speaking.instructions:
Listen. Then say each line out loud.
I was cooking when the power went off.
I was waiting at the entrance when the taxi arrived.
She was walking down the stairs when the lift stopped.
They were washing the floor when the manager came in.
We were standing in the doorway when it started to rain.
Now say the same five with while at the front.
While I was cooking, the power went off.
Leave a small pause where the comma is.
Tap the mic. Say all ten lines.
Tap the mic again and listen back.
Check: did every long part have was or were and -ing?
Check: did every short part have a past form and no -ing?
Check: did you pause after the while part each time?
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor to give you five long actions, each beginning with I was. Finish each one out loud with when and a short event.

speaking.title: Speaking 3 — Which place, which day
speaking.instructions:
Listen. Then say each line out loud.
The shop where I bought it was near the station.
That is the building where I work.
I still remember the morning when the lift stopped.
This is the yard where we leave the tools.
Nobody forgets the day when it happened.
Now make six of your own.
Three with where: a shop, a building, a yard.
Three with when: a day, a morning, a year.
They can be real or made up.
Tap the mic. Say all six.
Tap the mic again and listen back.
Check: did you say the noun first, then where or when, then the rest?
Check: did you leave the word there or then on the end? Take it off and say the line again.
Check: did you pause in the middle as if there were commas? There are none, so say it in one breath.
speaking.tutor: Say three of your where sentences to the tutor. Ask it which place each one is about, and see whether it names the right one.

speaking.title: Speaking 4 — When, where, exactly where, which way
speaking.instructions:
Four questions, always in this order. When? Where? Exactly where? Which way?
Listen to the model.
At six, in the yard, I was standing behind the fence.
Then I walked across the yard and out through the doorway.
Now build three of your own, one question at a time.
Start each one with a time: at six, on Monday, in the morning, during the shift.
Add a place: in the basement, at the entrance, on the roof.
Add a position: under the stairs, behind the fence, at the top of the steps.
End with a direction: up the stairs, out of the basement, towards the exit.
Tap the mic. Say all three.
Tap the mic again and listen back with the four questions in front of you.
Check: one small word for each question, and all four in every account.
If you hear in six o'clock, say the line again with at.
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor to give you a place and a time. Build one sentence with all four kinds of small word, then ask it which word answered which question.

speaking.title: Speaking 5 — Listen, then work out the word
speaking.instructions:
Go to Reading 1, The Morning the Lift Stopped.
Do not read it yet. Tap Listen and listen once, with your eyes closed.
Three words in it may be new: solution, consequence, detail.
After one listen, say out loud what you think each one means.
Tap the mic while you say your three meanings.
Say why: what was said just before it, and just after it.
Now open Reading 1 and read those three lines.
Tap the mic again and listen back to your recording.
Check: did you get the solution as the thing that ended the problem?
Check: did you get the consequence as something that happened later, because of it?
Check: did you get the detail as one small piece of information?
If one was wrong, listen to the text once more and say that meaning again.
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor to use solution, consequence and detail in three new sentences. Work out each meaning from its sentence before you ask whether you were right.

speaking.title: Speaking 6 — Two minutes: what happened
speaking.instructions:
Tell one account of the past, out loud, for two minutes.
It can be real or made up.
Plan it in four parts, one line each.
The scene: when and where. What was already happening. The event. One detail, and what came afterwards.
Use initially, meanwhile and shortly after to join the parts.
Use at least five words from this unit.
Use at least two sentences with was or were and -ing.
Tap the mic and talk for two minutes. Do not stop to fix a word.
Tap the mic again and listen back with this checklist.
Four parts, in order? Two long actions with -ing? Five unit words?
Did a listener who was not there learn when, where and what?
If you stopped more than three times, plan the four lines again and record once more.
speaking.tutor: Say your four planning lines to the tutor and ask it one thing: which part of your account a listener would still be confused about.

writing.title: Writing 1 — Eight sentences, eight past forms
writing.prompt:
Write 8 sentences about the past.
Each one uses a different verb from the first word group: teach, throw, spend, build, hide, shake, wear, lead.
Every verb must be in its past form.
They can be about a real day or a made-up one.
writing.model:
A colleague taught me the job in two days.
I threw the empty box into the bin by the exit.
We spent an hour at the entrance, waiting for the rain to stop.
They built the fence round the yard last summer.
Somebody hid the tools under the stairs.
The whole doorway shook when the storm started.
I wore a helmet in the basement all morning.
The cleaner led us out through the back exit.
writing.criteria:
8 sentences, one for each of the 8 verbs.
Every verb in its past form: taught, threw, spent, built, hid, shook, wore, led.
No -ed on any of these 8.
A capital letter at the start and a full stop at the end of each line.
At least 3 sentences that also name a place from group 3.
writing.support:
Write the 8 past forms down the page first, one per line: taught, threw, spent, built, hid, shook, wore, led.
Then put a person in front of each one.
Then add the rest of the sentence.
writing.extension: Turn 2 of your sentences into questions with did, and watch the verb go back to its plain form: Did she teach you the job?

writing.title: Writing 2 — Six times you say which one
writing.prompt:
Write 6 sentences.
3 of them name a place with where: the shop where I bought it.
3 of them name a time with when: the day when it happened.
Each sentence must say something more after the where or when part.
The places and the times can be real or made up.
writing.model:
The shop where I bought this bag closed last month.
That is the building where I work on Tuesdays.
This is the yard where we leave the tools every night.
I still remember the morning when the lift stopped.
The day when it happened was wet and cold.
They built the fence in the year when the road opened.
writing.criteria:
6 sentences: 3 with where, 3 with when.
The noun comes first, then where or when, then the rest.
No commas inside the where or when part.
No extra there or then on the end.
Every sentence says something more after that part.
writing.support:
Write the 6 nouns first: shop, building, yard, morning, day, year.
Ask of each one: is it a place or a time? Place takes where, time takes when.
Then write the small fact that says which one you mean.
Then add what happened.
writing.extension: Add a seventh sentence about a person, using who: the woman who led us out.

writing.title: Writing 3 — One account, in four parts
writing.prompt:
Write one account of something that happened, in 4 short parts.
1. The scene: when and where.
2. What was already happening, with was or were and -ing.
3. The event: one short sentence in the past form.
4. One detail, and what happened afterwards.
It can be real or made up, and it does not have to be about you.
writing.model:
At ten past eight on Monday, I was at the entrance of a building with six floors.
It was raining hard, and I was waiting for the lift with a wet bag.
The lift shook once and stopped between two floors.
The detail I remember is the notice on the wall, which nobody read.
Shortly after that, a woman in a blue uniform opened the doors and led me out.
Meanwhile, everybody else was walking up the wet stairs.
writing.length: Four short parts, six to eight sentences in all
writing.criteria:
4 parts, in that order.
At least 1 sentence with was or were and -ing.
At least 1 sentence with when or while, with a comma if the while part comes first.
At least 3 small words answering When, Where, Exactly where and Which way.
At least 4 words from this unit.
A capital letter and a full stop on every sentence.
writing.support:
Write 4 single words first, one for each part: the time, the place, the thing that was already happening, the thing that happened.
Then grow each word into one sentence.
Add the detail last, when the rest is already on the page.
writing.extension: Add one sentence with where or when inside it: the doorway where I stood, or the morning when it happened.

writing.title: Writing 4 — Check your own account, line by line
writing.prompt:
Take your Writing 3 account and read it 4 times, once for each question.
1. Is every long action written with was or were and -ing?
2. Is there a comma after the while part when it comes first, and none inside a where or when part?
3. Are the past forms right: taught, threw, spent, built, hid, shook, wore, led?
4. Does every small word answer When, Where, Exactly where or Which way?
Mark every line you change. Count them at the end.
writing.model:
Before: While I was waiting the lift shook and stopped.
After: While I was waiting, the lift shook and stopped.

Before: She teached me what to do on the stairs.
After: She taught me what to do on the stairs.

Before: We met in six o'clock at the entrance.
After: We met at six o'clock at the entrance.

Before: The shop where I bought it there was near the station.
After: The shop where I bought it was near the station.
writing.starter: Question 1: I read the whole account and I changed …
writing.length: Four readings of your own account, and a count of your changes
writing.criteria:
4 readings, one question each.
Every changed line marked.
A number at the end: how many lines you changed.
At least 1 change under question 1 or question 2.
The account still says the same thing afterwards.
writing.support:
Do one question at a time over the whole account, not all four questions on one line.
For question 1, read the account out loud. Your ear hears a missing was before your eye sees it.
writing.extension: Record yourself reading the corrected account. Anything you stumble over is usually a sentence that wants cutting in two.

activities.title: Practice 1 — The eight past forms
activities.instructions:
Write the past form of the verb in brackets.
1. A colleague ______ (teach) me the job on my first shift.
2. She ______ (throw) the empty box into the yard.
3. We ______ (spend) all morning on one form.
4. They ______ (build) the basement before the rest of the building.
5. Somebody ______ (hide) the tools under the stairs.
6. The doorway ______ (shake) when the storm started.
7. He ______ (wear) the same uniform for ten years.
8. The cleaner ______ (lead) us out through the back exit.
activities.answers:
1. taught
2. threw
3. spent
4. built
5. hid
6. shook
7. wore
8. led
Items 5 and 8 are the short ones people get wrong: hid has one d, and led has one e.
7 or 8 right: you have all eight. 5 or 6: say the pairs out loud and do it again.
4 or fewer: write the eight pairs on paper, cover the past forms, and test yourself twice before you come back.
activities.solo: Say each finished sentence out loud before you write it. Then check against the key and count the right ones.

activities.title: Practice 2 — Long action or short event
activities.instructions:
Write was, were with the -ing form, or the past form.
1. I ______ (stand) in the doorway when the taxi arrived.
2. While she ______ (carry) the box down the stairs, she dropped it.
3. They were washing the floor when the manager ______ (come) in.
4. We ______ (wait) at the entrance when it started to rain.
5. He was walking across the yard when somebody ______ (shout).
6. While I ______ (look) for the key, the door shook.
7. She ______ (lead) us out while the lights were going off.
8. I ______ (cook) when the power went off.
activities.answers:
1. was standing
2. was carrying
3. came
4. were waiting
5. shouted
6. was looking
7. led
8. was cooking
Items 3, 5 and 7 are the short events. Each one happened once, quickly, so each one takes the past form and no -ing.
7 or 8 right: you can tell the two apart. 5 or 6: ask of every line, which one was already running?
4 or fewer: read the Pattern 2 worked example again, line by line, then do 1 to 4 once more.
activities.solo: Before you write, say out loud which action was already running. Then write, then check against the key and count.

activities.title: Practice 3 — Where, when, who or that
activities.instructions:
Write where, when, who or that.
1. That is the building ______ I work.
2. I remember the morning ______ the lift stopped.
3. This is the yard ______ we leave the tools.
4. The woman ______ led us out was wearing a blue uniform.
5. The box ______ I dropped was full of paper.
6. They built the fence in the year ______ the road opened.
7. Nobody forgets the day ______ it happened.
8. The café ______ I left my bag closed at six.
activities.answers:
1. where
2. when
3. where
4. who
5. that
6. when
7. when
8. where
The test is one question: is the word before the gap a place, a time, a person or a thing?
Item 6 catches people out. A year is a time, not a place, so it takes when.
7 or 8 right: go on. 5 or 6: write P, T, PE or TH above each noun first, then fill the gaps.
4 or fewer: read the Pattern 3 rule out loud, one block at a time.
activities.solo: Cover the key. Write your eight answers, then write beside each one whether the noun was a place, a time, a person or a thing. Then uncover the key.

activities.title: Practice 4 — Four questions, four small words
activities.instructions:
Write the missing small word. Ask yourself which question it answers.
1. The shift started ______ six ______ the morning.
2. We waited ______ the entrance ______ Monday.
3. He hid the box ______ the fence, where nobody could see it.
4. She led us ______ of the basement and ______ the stairs.
5. I carried the bag ______ the yard and ______ the exit.
6. The tools are ______ the top ______ the stairs.
7. Two people were working ______ the roof ______ the storm.
8. He walked ______ the doorway and ______ the yard.
activities.answers:
1. at, in
2. at, on
3. behind
4. out, up
5. across, towards
6. at, of
7. on, during
8. through, into
Item 1 is the usual slip: a clock time takes at, and a part of the day takes in. Only at night is different.
Item 8 is the other one: through is the way you pass a doorway, and into is where you end up.
7 or 8 right: you can build an account now. 5 or 6: ask the four questions on each line in order.
4 or fewer: read the Pattern 4 rule and say every example out loud once.
activities.solo: Write the question above each gap first: When, Where, Exactly where or Which way. Then fill the gaps, then check the key and count.

activities.title: Practice 5 — Put the account in order
activities.instructions:
These six lines tell one account, in the wrong order.
Write them in the right order, 1 to 6. The time words tell you where each one goes.
a. Shortly after that, a cleaner took the box out and the doors closed.
b. Initially, nobody knew why the lift had stopped.
c. Beforehand, nobody looked at the doorway on the fourth floor.
d. Meanwhile, everybody else in the building was walking up the wet stairs.
e. At ten past eight, the lift shook once and stopped between two floors.
f. The consequence was a notice on the wall, which is still there.
Then answer these two.
7. Which line happened before all the others?
8. Which line tells you about something happening at the same time as another line?
activities.answers:
1c, 2e, 3b, 4d, 5a, 6f.
7. Line c. Beforehand means before the time you are talking about, so it comes before the lift stops.
8. Line d. Meanwhile means at the same time as something else, so it sits beside line b rather than after it.
The line people put in the wrong place is c. Beforehand looks like a middle word and is always an early one.
5 or 6 right: the time words are doing their job for you. 3 or 4: read the six time words again in the fourth word group.
2 or fewer: put the two easy ones first, at ten past eight and the consequence, then fit the rest between them.
activities.solo: Do it with the word group closed. Then open the fourth group, read the six meanings, and mark your own order against them.

activities.title: Practice 6 — Find the mistake
activities.instructions:
Each line has one mistake. Write it correctly and say what was wrong.
1. She teached me the job in two days.
2. I cooked when the power went off.
3. While I was waiting the lift shook and stopped.
4. We met in six o'clock at the entrance.
5. The shop where I bought it there was near the station.
6. Did she taught you the job?
7. I went in the basement to find the tools.
8. The doorway, where I stood, was wet.
activities.answers:
1. She taught me the job in two days. teach does not take -ed.
2. I was cooking when the power went off. The long action needs was and -ing.
3. While I was waiting, the lift shook and stopped. The comma after the while part was missing.
4. We met at six o'clock at the entrance. A clock time takes at.
5. The shop where I bought it was near the station. where already means in that place, so there goes.
6. Did she teach you the job? did carries the past, so the verb beside it is plain.
7. I went into the basement to find the tools. Movement takes into.
8. The doorway where I stood was wet. This part says which doorway, so it keeps no commas.
Items 3 and 8 are two halves of one rule: a comma goes in after a while part at the front, and never inside a where or when part.
7 or 8 right: you can check your own writing now. 5 or 6: read all four mistake boxes again.
4 or fewer: do Practices 1 to 4 once more before you come back to this one.
activities.solo: Write your eight corrected lines first. Then read the key and tick each one you got. Copy out twice any line you missed.

quizzes.q: She ______ me the job in two days.
quizzes.why: teach does not add -ed. Its past form is taught. Teached is the tempting one, because most verbs really do add -ed, but these eight change shape instead. Teachs is not a word, and was teach has no -ing on the end.

quizzes.q: I ______ down the stairs when the lift stopped.
quizzes.why: Walking down the stairs took time, so it is the long action and takes was with -ing. Walked and went are past forms, and they would make the walking a short event, which it was not. Walking on its own has no was in front of it.

quizzes.q: The shop ______ I bought it was near the station.
quizzes.why: A shop is a place, and a place takes where. When names a time, who names a person, and what cannot be used here at all.
A clock time takes at: at six o'clock. In goes with a part of the day or a month: in the morning, in May. On goes with a day: on Monday. During goes with something that lasts: during the shift.

options: Did she taught you the job?
Did she teach you the job?
Did she teaches you the job?
She did taught you the job?
quizzes.a: Did she teach you the job?
quizzes.why: did already carries the past, so the verb beside it goes back to its plain form: teach. The first option keeps the past form as well, which is the commonest slip. The third adds an s that belongs to the present, and the fourth is not a question at all.

quizzes.q: She ______ us out of the basement.
quizzes.why: The past form of lead is led, with one e. Leaded and leded are both attempts to add -ed, and neither is English. Was led would mean somebody took her, not that she took us.

quizzes.q: Which sentence puts the comma in the right place?
options: I was cooking, when the power went off.
While I was cooking the power went off.
While, I was cooking the power went off.
While I was cooking, the power went off.
quizzes.a: While I was cooking, the power went off.
quizzes.why: The comma goes in only when the while part comes first, and it goes at the end of that part. The first option needs no comma at all, because the while part is not at the front. The second is missing it, and the third puts it straight after while, where nothing has been said yet.

quizzes.q: I went ______ the basement to find the tools.
quizzes.why: This is movement from outside to inside, and movement takes into. In would say where you already were, not where you went. On and at cannot be used for going inside a place.

quizzes.q: The lift stopped and nobody could get out. That was the ______ .
quizzes.why: The situation is how things are at one moment, especially when there is a problem, and that is what this sentence describes. The solution would be the thing that ended it. A detail is one small piece of information, and a consequence is something that happens later because of it.

quizzes.q: I still remember the day ______ it happened.
quizzes.why: A day is a time, and a time takes when. Where names a place. Which is for a thing, and a day here is not a thing you point at. That is would start a new sentence instead of joining this one.

quizzes.q: The incident record says never to leave anything in a lift doorway, on any floor. What does that mean for a person carrying a box on floor 2?
options: They can put it down, because the record is about floor 4.
They must report it at the desk before they put it down.
They can leave it there for one shift only.
They must not put it down in the doorway at all.
quizzes.a: They must not put it down in the doorway at all.
quizzes.why: The record says on any floor, so floor 2 is included, and anything in the doorway stops the doors closing. The first option reads the floor number and ignores the words after it. Reporting is for after an incident, and nothing in the record allows one shift or any other length of time.

quizzes.q: In Reading 1 the incident has one consequence. What does consequence mean there?
options: The reason the lift stopped in the first place.
Something that happened later, because of the incident.
The person who fixed the problem.
One small piece of information about the incident.
quizzes.a: Something that happened later, because of the incident.
quizzes.why: Everything after the word came later and came from the incident: everybody used the stairs, the stairs were wet, and a notice went up. The reason is the cause, not the consequence, and the two point in opposite directions. The third option describes a person, and the fourth is what detail means.

teacherNotes.note: Adding -ed to the eight irregular verbs is the error to expect, and it is a sign of progress rather than carelessness: the learner has generalised the -ed rule, which is exactly what they were asked to do in an earlier unit. The fix that works is saying the pair aloud rather than reading the single word, which is why Speaking 1 drills teach, taught before it drills any sentence. Practice 1 items 5 and 8 are where the short forms hid and led slip, and the key names the spelling rather than just correcting it.

The second error is putting both halves in the past form: I cooked when the power went off. It is not a tense error so much as a picture error, so the fix is a question rather than a rule. Which one was already running? Pattern 2's worked example asks that question first and only then chooses the form, and Practice 2 mixes long and short actions in one list so the question has to be asked on every line.

Commas cause trouble in two opposite directions in this unit, and they are deliberately taught side by side. A while part at the front takes a comma after it; a where or when part takes none, ever, because it says which one you mean and cannot be lifted out. Practice 6 items 3 and 8 are the same rule twice, in both directions, and the key says so, so the learner sees one idea and not two corrections.

Every card shows one item worked through before its practice. Every practice carries a key with a score line and a named next step. Every speaking task ends with record, listen back and a checklist the learner can see, and Speaking 5 checks itself against Reading 1 rather than against an opinion. Writing 4 is the only task with no separate key, because it is the learner reading their own account against four questions and counting their own changes.

The incident in this unit is small on purpose: a box in a doorway, a lift that stopped, eleven minutes. Nobody is hurt, nothing is anybody's fault, and no blame is named in any of the three texts. That is partly kindness and partly grammar, because an account with an opinion in it stops being a sequence of past events and becomes an argument, which is a Stage 6 job. Reading 2 says so out loud, and the assignment asks for the same restraint.

selfAssessment.statement: I can write about the past with verbs like taught, threw and hid.
I can say what I was doing when something happened.
I can say which place I mean: the shop where I bought it.
I can say when and where it happened: at six, in the yard, up the stairs.
I can work out what a new word means from the words around it.
I can work out what a new word means when I hear it in a story.
I can plan, write and check a short account of something that happened.
I can tell a two-minute story about the past so that somebody can follow it.

assignment.title: What happened that morning
assignment.instructions:
Tell one account of something that happened. It can be real or made up, and it does not have to be about you.
Part 1. Write the account.
Write it in 4 parts, in this order.
1. The scene: when and where. Use at least 2 small words, one for the time and one for the place.
2. What was already happening. At least 1 sentence with was or were and -ing.
3. The event. One short sentence in the past form, joined with when or while.
4. One detail, and what happened afterwards. Join it with initially, meanwhile or shortly after.
Use at least 3 past forms from the first word group: taught, threw, spent, built, hid, shook, wore, led.
Use at least 1 sentence that says which place or which day: the doorway where I stood, the morning when it happened.
Part 2. Record yourself.
Say the same account out loud, in the same 4 parts. Keep it under two minutes.
Do not read your writing word for word. Look at your 4 part headings and talk.
Part 3. Check your own work before you finish.
Read the written account 4 times, once for each question.
Is every long action was or were and -ing? Is the comma after the while part and nowhere inside a where or when part?
Are the past forms right? Does every small word answer When, Where, Exactly where or Which way?
Then listen back to the recording once with your writing in front of you.
Count: 4 parts, 3 past forms, 1 where or when sentence, 2 small words in part 1.
If something is missing, add it and record Part 2 again.
assignment.submissionType: A written account and an audio recording of the same account
